messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mikaere Tupu, a 46-year-old widowed auditor of Māori and Samoan background, came to treatment months after a cyclone tore through the coastal town where he and his wife had lived. During the storm, the house shook so violently that he could hear the roof panels slamming and, outside, the strange silence between gusts before the next surge of wind and water. He lost power, phone service, and then his wife, who was swept away when they tried to reach higher ground. In the chaotic hours that followed, the smell of brackish mud and splintered timber, and the bitter taste of dirty water and fuel, seemed to lodge in him. Even now, when the memory comes back, Mikaere says it is hard to believe it happened to him at all; it feels too extreme, like something he watched happen to someone else. Yet the memory is not distant. At night, especially when he wakes in the dark, the smell of damp sludge can rush back, and with it the taste he remembers from the floodwater, as if his body is replaying the disaster before he can think.

In the weeks after the cyclone, Mikaere began to notice that moments of ease were not restful for him but dangerous. If he found himself feeling happy for a few minutes—at work after finishing a difficult audit, or at home when a conversation with his sister briefly lifted his mood—he would suddenly feel exposed, as though calm invited punishment. Those moments were followed by a sharp pull into smoking, stepping outside for cigarette after cigarette, and by a reflex to shut down any chance of talking about what had happened. He avoided conversations with neighbors about the storm’s aftermath, and when coworkers asked how he was managing, he gave a brief nod and changed the subject. He had come to believe that if he let himself relax, something terrible would happen again, and that belief made even ordinary warmth feel unsafe. The more he protected himself by smoking, avoiding rest, and keeping silent, the more he felt his world narrowing around the same thought: he could not stop bad things from happening to him. That sense of helplessness deepened his conviction that the world was dangerous and left him feeling dead inside, as if whatever had been vibrant in him before the cyclone had been drained away.

The more numb and helpless Mikaere felt, the more his mind seemed to scan for danger. Unfamiliar places became intolerable because he could not assess what might happen there, so he stopped taking new routes for work and avoided visiting clients in offices he did not know well. At home, unusual silence could jolt him immediately; if the neighborhood went quiet or if a meeting at the office dragged on longer than expected, he assumed something bad was unfolding just beyond view. Those expectations were not abstract. They were tied to the disaster itself, when the air had gone eerily still before the next violent blast of wind, and when delays in hearing from emergency services had felt like confirmation that help would not come. Once that kind of threat state was active, his memory became more vivid and invasive. A quiet room could bring the smell of wet earth back to him, and the taste of salt and fuel, and those sensations made the world around him seem newly menacing. Even a brief moment of happiness, a softer evening at home, could pull him back into the storm in miniature, as if his body mistrusted peace and kept searching for the next collapse.

To manage all of this, Mikaere clung to habits that seemed protective in the short term but kept feeding the pattern. He smoked to steady himself, avoided relaxing because stillness felt dangerous, and refused to talk in any depth about his wife’s death or the aftermath. Those strategies gave him the illusion of control, but they also kept his grief and fear unprocessed, and that only strengthened the belief that he was permanently unsafe and on his own. The more he withdrew, the more unfamiliar even ordinary places felt, and the more silence, delay, or a sudden good mood at work could trigger the sense that danger was near. His avoidance also meant that his days remained organized around escape rather than recovery; he stopped meeting friends after work, declined invitations to family gatherings, and became less available in his role as an auditor because he could not tolerate being sent somewhere unpredictable. By the time he presented for help, he was sleeping poorly, waking into darkness with his heart racing, and spending much of the day braced for the next sign that disaster was about to strike. What finally brought Mikaere in was the fear that he was disappearing into a life built around smoke, silence, and vigilance, and he said he was hoping, more than anything, to feel safe enough to rest without waiting for the world to break again.
